# zeroize - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/zeroize/^1.8/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#rustcrypto-zeroize)[RustCrypto](https://github.com/RustCrypto): zeroize

Securely zero memory (a.k.a. [zeroize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeroisation)) while avoiding compiler optimizations.

This crate implements a portable approach to securely zeroing memory using techniques which guarantee they won’t be “optimized away” by the compiler.

The [ Zeroize trait](https://docs.rs/zeroize/latest/zeroize/trait.Zeroize.html) is the crate’s primary API.

[§](https://docs.rs#about)About

[Zeroing memory securely is hard](http://www.daemonology.net/blog/2014-09-04-how-to-zero-a-buffer.html) - compilers optimize for performance, and
in doing so they love to “optimize away” unnecessary zeroing calls. There are
many documented “tricks” to attempt to avoid these optimizations and ensure
that a zeroing routine is performed reliably.

This crate isn’t about tricks: it uses [core::ptr::write_volatile](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/ptr/fn.write_volatile.html)
and [core::sync::atomic](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/core/sync/atomic/index.html) memory fences to provide easy-to-use, portable
zeroing behavior which works on all of Rust’s core number types and slices
thereof, implemented in pure Rust with no usage of FFI or assembly.

- No insecure fallbacks!
- No dependencies!
- No FFI or inline assembly! **WASM friendly**(and tested)!
- `#![no_std]`i.e.- **embedded-friendly**!
- No functionality besides securely zeroing memory!
- (Optional) Custom derive support for zeroing complex structures

[§](https://docs.rs#minimum-supported-rust-version)Minimum Supported Rust Version

Requires Rust **1.85** or newer.

In the future, we reserve the right to change MSRV (i.e. MSRV is out-of-scope for this crate’s semantic versioning guarantees).

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use zeroize::Zeroize;
// Protip: don't embed secrets in your source code.
// This is just an example.
let mut secret = b"Air shield password: 1,2,3,4,5".to_vec();
// [ ... ] open the air shield here
// Now that we're done using the secret, zero it out.
secret.zeroize();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#license)License

Licensed under either of:

at your option.

[§](https://docs.rs#contribution)Contribution

Unless you explicitly state otherwise, any contribution intentionally submitted for inclusion in the work by you, as defined in the Apache-2.0 license, shall be dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

[§](https://docs.rs#traits)Traits

The [ Zeroize](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroize.html) trait is the core API of this crate. It’s intended to be impl’d on values that
may-or-may-not contain secrets, for example the

`zeroize` crate itself defines them on the
core integers e.g. `u8`, `u16`, `i8`, `i16`, as well as arrays thereof. Its core API is
[, a method which takes](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroize.html#tymethod.zeroize)

`Zeroize::zeroize``&mut self` and writes over the type’s internal
memory with some placeholder value, typically some form of `0`.The [ DefaultIsZeroes](https://docs.rs/trait.DefaultIsZeroes.html) marker trait can be impl’d on types which have a

[impl that can be used for](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/default/trait.Default.html)

`Default`[. Types which implement this trait receive a blanket impl of the](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroize.html)

`Zeroize`[trait.](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroize.html)

`Zeroize`We recommend that types which always contain secrets, and especially ones which need to maintain
complex invariants, do NOT impl the [ Zeroize](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroize.html) trait, but instead provide a

[impl which takes care of erasing the secret values from memory directly. Such types can mark that they’re doing this with the](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/drop/trait.Drop.html)

`Drop`[marker trait. Note that](https://docs.rs/trait.ZeroizeOnDrop.html)

`ZeroizeOnDrop`[is](https://docs.rs/trait.ZeroizeOnDrop.html)

`ZeroizeOnDrop`*just*a marker trait, and making it actually work requires actually providing a

[impl which takes care of zeroizing secrets.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/drop/trait.Drop.html)

`Drop`Why not impl [ Zeroize](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroize.html) for such types, e.g. a

`SecretKey` type? The problem is [would effectively leave such types in an invalid state, and a sort of use-after-zeroize condition becomes possible. For that reason, we recommend these types automatically handle zeroization in their](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroize.html)

`Zeroize`[handler alone.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/drop/trait.Drop.html)

`Drop`[§](https://docs.rs#supported-types)Supported types

The [ Zeroize](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroize.html) trait is impl’d on all of Rust’s core scalar types including
integers, floats,

`bool`, and `char`.Additionally, it’s implemented on slices and `IterMut`s of the above types.

When the `alloc` feature is enabled (which it is by default), it’s also
impl’d for `Vec<T>` for the above types as well as `String`, where it provides
[ Vec::clear](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html#method.clear) /

[-like behavior (truncating to zero-length) but ensures the backing memory is securely zeroed with some caveats.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html#method.clear)

`String::clear`With the `std` feature enabled (which it is **not** by default), [ Zeroize](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroize.html)
is also implemented for

[. After calling](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/ffi/struct.CString.html)

`CString``zeroize()` on a `CString`,
its internal buffer will contain exactly one nul byte. The backing
memory is zeroed by converting it to a `Vec<u8>` and back into a `CString`.
(NOTE: see “Stack/Heap Zeroing Notes” for important `Vec`/`String`/`CString` details)The [ DefaultIsZeroes](https://docs.rs/trait.DefaultIsZeroes.html) marker trait can be impl’d on types which also
impl

[, which implements](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/default/trait.Default.html)

`Default`[by overwriting a value with the default value.](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroize.html)

`Zeroize`[§](https://docs.rs#custom-derive-support)Custom Derive Support

This crate has custom derive support for the `Zeroize` trait,
gated under the `zeroize` crate’s `zeroize_derive` Cargo feature,
which automatically calls `zeroize()` on all members of a struct
or tuple struct.

Attributes supported for `Zeroize`:

On the item level:

- `#[zeroize(drop)]`:- *deprecated*use- `ZeroizeOnDrop`instead
- `#[zeroize(bound = "T: MyTrait")]`: this replaces any trait bounds inferred by zeroize

On the field level:

- `#[zeroize(skip)]`: skips this field or variant when calling- `zeroize()`

Attributes supported for `ZeroizeOnDrop`:

On the field level:

- `#[zeroize(skip)]`: skips this field or variant when calling- `zeroize()`

Example which derives `Drop`:

```
use zeroize::{Zeroize, ZeroizeOnDrop};
// This struct will be zeroized on drop
#[derive(Zeroize, ZeroizeOnDrop)]
struct MyStruct([u8; 32]);
```
Example which does not derive `Drop` (useful for e.g. `Copy` types)

```
#[cfg(feature = "zeroize_derive")]
use zeroize::Zeroize;
// This struct will *NOT* be zeroized on drop
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Zeroize)]
struct MyStruct([u8; 32]);
```
Example which only derives `Drop`:

```
use zeroize::ZeroizeOnDrop;
// This struct will be zeroized on drop
#[derive(ZeroizeOnDrop)]
struct MyStruct([u8; 32]);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#zeroizingz-wrapper-for-zeroizing-arbitrary-values-on-drop)`Zeroizing<Z>`: wrapper for zeroizing arbitrary values on drop

`Zeroizing<Z: Zeroize>` is a generic wrapper type that impls `Deref`
and `DerefMut`, allowing access to an inner value of type `Z`, and also
impls a `Drop` handler which calls `zeroize()` on its contents:

```
use zeroize::Zeroizing;
fn use_secret() {
    let mut secret = Zeroizing::new([0u8; 5]);
    // Set the air shield password
    // Protip (again): don't embed secrets in your source code.
    secret.copy_from_slice(&[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]);
    assert_eq!(secret.as_ref(), &[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]);
    // The contents of `secret` will be automatically zeroized on drop
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#what-guarantees-does-this-crate-provide)What guarantees does this crate provide?

This crate guarantees the zeroing operation can’t be “optimized away” by the compiler, as ensured by LLVM’s volatile semantics.

Previously there were worries that the approach used by this crate (mixing volatile and
non-volatile accesses) was undefined behavior due to language contained
in the documentation for `write_volatile`, however after some discussion
within the [Unsafe Code Guidelines Working Group](https://github.com/rust-lang/unsafe-code-guidelines), [these remarks have been removed](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/60972) and the
specific usage pattern in this crate is considered to be well-defined.

All of that said, there is still potential for microarchitectural attacks (ala Spectre/Meltdown) to leak “zeroized” secrets through covert channels. This crate makes no guarantees that zeroized values cannot be leaked through such channels, as they represent flaws in the underlying hardware.

[§](https://docs.rs#stackheap-zeroing-notes)Stack/Heap Zeroing Notes

This crate can be used to zero values from either the stack or the heap. We recommend storing sensitive data on the heap whenever possible to reduce the potential for making copies in memory via Rust move semantics, however note that stack spilling and other optimizations may leave temporary copies of data from the heap on the stack.

[ zeroize_stack](https://docs.rs/fn.zeroize_stack.html) can be used to zeroize stack memory.

[ Pin](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/pin/struct.Pin.html) can be leveraged in conjunction with this crate to ensure data kept
on the stack isn’t moved.

The `Zeroize` impls for `Vec`, `String` and `CString` zeroize the entire capacity of their
backing buffer, but cannot guarantee copies of the data were not previously made by buffer
reallocation. It’s therefore important when attempting to zeroize such buffers to initialize
them to the correct capacity, and take care to prevent subsequent reallocation.

The [ secrecy](https://docs.rs/secrecy) crate provides higher-level abstractions for eliminating
usage patterns which can cause reallocations:

[§](https://docs.rs#what-about-clearing-registers-mlock-mprotect-etc)What about: clearing registers, `mlock()`, `mprotect()`, etc?

This crate is focused on providing simple, unobtrusive support for reliably zeroing memory using the best approach possible on stable Rust.

Clearing registers is a difficult problem that can’t easily be solved by
something like a crate, and requires either inline ASM or rustc support.
See [https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/17046](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/17046) for background on
this particular problem.

Other memory protection mechanisms are interesting and useful, but often overkill (e.g. defending against RAM scraping or attackers with swap access). In as much as there may be merit to these approaches, there are also many other crates that already implement more sophisticated memory protections. Such protections are explicitly out-of-scope for this crate.

Zeroing memory is [good cryptographic hygiene](https://github.com/veorq/cryptocoding#clean-memory-of-secret-data) and this crate seeks to promote
it in the most unobtrusive manner possible. This includes omitting complex
`unsafe` memory protection systems and just trying to make the best memory
zeroing crate available.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Zeroizing](https://docs.rs/struct.Zeroizing.html)
- `Zeroizing`is a wrapper for any- `Z: Zeroize`type which implements a- `Drop`handler which zeroizes dropped values.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits-1)

- Fallible trait for representing cases where zeroization may or may not be possible.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [optimization_](https://docs.rs/fn.optimization_barrier.html)- barrier
- Observe the referenced data and prevent the compiler from removing previous writes to it.
- [zeroize_](https://docs.rs/fn.zeroize_flat_type.html)- flat_ - type - ⚠

dynamically sized values or trait objects. It would be inefficient to use this function on a

# pretty_assertions - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/pretty_assertions/^1.4.1/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#pretty-assertions)Pretty Assertions

When writing tests in Rust, you’ll probably use `assert_eq!(a, b)` *a lot*.

If such a test fails, it will present all the details of `a` and `b`.
But you have to spot the differences yourself, which is not always straightforward,
like here:

Wouldn’t that task be *much* easier with a colorful diff?

Yep — and you only need **one line of code** to make it happen:

`use pretty_assertions::{assert_eq, assert_ne};`## Show the example behind the screenshots above.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// 1. add the `pretty_assertions` dependency to `Cargo.toml`.
// 2. insert this line at the top of each module, as needed
use pretty_assertions::{assert_eq, assert_ne};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]
struct Foo {
    lorem: &'static str,
    ipsum: u32,
    dolor: Result<String, String>,
}
let x = Some(Foo { lorem: "Hello World!", ipsum: 42, dolor: Ok("hey".to_string())});
let y = Some(Foo { lorem: "Hello Wrold!", ipsum: 42, dolor: Ok("hey ho!".to_string())});
assert_eq!(x, y);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#tip)Tip

Specify it as [ [dev-dependencies]](http://doc.crates.io/specifying-dependencies.html#development-dependencies)
and it will only be used for compiling tests, examples, and benchmarks.
This way the compile time of

`cargo build` won’t be affected!Also add `#[cfg(test)]` to your `use` statements, like this:

```
#[cfg(test)]
use pretty_assertions::{assert_eq, assert_ne};
```
[§](https://docs.rs#note)Note

- Since `Rust 2018`edition, you need to declare`use pretty_assertions::{assert_eq, assert_ne};`per module. Before you would write`#[macro_use] extern crate pretty_assertions;`.
- The replacement is only effective in your own crate, not in other libraries you include.
- `assert_ne`is also switched to multi-line presentation, but does- *not*show a diff.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

Features provided by the crate are:

- `std`: Use the Rust standard library. Enabled by default. Exactly one of- `std`and- `alloc`is required.
- `alloc`: Use the- `alloc`crate. Exactly one of- `std`and- `alloc`is required.
- `unstable`: opt-in to unstable features that may not follow Semantic Versioning. The implementation behind this feature is subject to change without warning between patch versions.

# tempfile - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tempfile/^3.23.0/

## Expand description

This is a library for creating temporary files and directories that are automatically deleted when no longer referenced (i.e., on drop).

- Use `tempfile()``std::fs::File`
- Use `NamedTempFile::new()`*named*temporary file that can be referred to its path.
- Use `tempdir()`
- Use `spooled_tempfile()`

[§](https://docs.rs#design)Design

This crate provides several approaches to creating temporary files and directories.
[ tempfile()](https://docs.rs/fn.tempfile.html) relies on the OS to remove the temporary file once the last handle is closed.

[and](https://docs.rs/struct.TempDir.html)

`TempDir`[both rely on Rust destructors for cleanup.](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedTempFile.html)

`NamedTempFile`[§](https://docs.rs#resource-leaking)Resource Leaking

`tempfile` will (almost) never fail to cleanup temporary resources. However `TempDir` and
`NamedTempFile` will fail if their destructors don’t run. This is because `tempfile` relies on
the OS to cleanup the underlying file, while `TempDir` and `NamedTempFile` rely on rust
destructors to do so. Destructors may fail to run if the process exits through an unhandled
signal interrupt (like `SIGINT`), or if the instance is declared statically (like with
[ lazy_static](https://github.com/rust-lang-nursery/lazy-static.rs/issues/62)), among other possible reasons.

[§](https://docs.rs#unexpected-file-deletion)Unexpected File Deletion

Most operating systems periodically clean up temporary files that haven’t been accessed recently
(often on the order of multiple days). This issue does not affect unnamed temporary files but
can invalidate the paths associated with named temporary files on Unix-like systems because the
temporary file can be unlinked from the filesystem while still open and in-use. See the
[temporary file cleaner](https://docs.rs#temporary-file-cleaners) section for more security implications.

[§](https://docs.rs#security)Security

This section discusses security issues relevant to Unix-like operating systems that use shared temporary directories by default. Importantly, it’s not relevant for Windows or macOS as both operating systems use private per-user temporary directories by default.

Applications can mitigate the issues described below by using [ env::override_temp_dir](https://docs.rs/env/fn.override_temp_dir.html) to
change the default temporary directory but should do so if and only if default the temporary
directory (

[) is unsuitable (is world readable, world writable, managed by a temporary file cleaner, etc.).](https://docs.rs/env/fn.temp_dir.html)

`env::temp_dir`[§](https://docs.rs#temporary-file-cleaners)Temporary File Cleaners

In the presence of pathological temporary file cleaner, relying on file paths is unsafe because a temporary file cleaner could delete the temporary file which an attacker could then replace.

This isn’t an issue for [ tempfile](https://docs.rs/fn.tempfile.html) as it doesn’t rely on file paths. However,

[and temporary directories](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedTempFile.html)

`NamedTempFile`*do*rely on file paths for

*some*operations. See the security documentation on the

[and the](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedTempFile.html)

`NamedTempFile`[types for more information.](https://docs.rs/struct.TempDir.html)

`TempDir`Mitigation:

- This is rarely an issue for short-lived files as temporary file cleaners usually only remove temporary files that haven’t been modified or accessed within many (10-30) days.
- Very long lived temporary files should be placed in directories not managed by temporary file cleaners.

[§](https://docs.rs#access-permissions)Access Permissions

Temporary *files* created with this library are private by default on all operating systems.
However, temporary *directories* are created with the default permissions and will therefore be
world-readable by default unless the user has changed their umask and/or default temporary
directory.

[§](https://docs.rs#denial-of-service)Denial of Service

If the file-name randomness ([ Builder::rand_bytes](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html#method.rand_bytes)) is too small and/or this crate is built
without the

`getrandom` feature, it may be possible for an attacker to predict the random file
names chosen by this library, preventing temporary file creation by creating temporary files
with these predicted file names. By default, this library mitigates this denial of service
attack by:- Defaulting to 6 random characters per temporary file forcing an attacker to create billions of files before random collisions are expected (at which point you probably have larger problems).
- Re-seeding the random filename generator from system randomness after 3 failed attempts to
create temporary a file (when the `getrandom`feature is enabled as it is by default on all major platforms).

[§](https://docs.rs#early-drop-pitfall)Early drop pitfall

Because `TempDir` and `NamedTempFile` rely on their destructors for cleanup, this can lead
to an unexpected early removal of the directory/file, usually when working with APIs which are
generic over `AsRef<Path>`. Consider the following example:

```
use tempfile::tempdir;
use std::process::Command;
// Create a directory inside of `env::temp_dir()`.
let temp_dir = tempdir()?;
// Spawn the `touch` command inside the temporary directory and collect the exit status
// Note that `temp_dir` is **not** moved into `current_dir`, but passed as a reference
let exit_status = Command::new("touch").arg("tmp").current_dir(&temp_dir).status()?;
assert!(exit_status.success());
```
This works because a reference to `temp_dir` is passed to `current_dir`, resulting in the
destructor of `temp_dir` being run after the `Command` has finished execution. Moving the
`TempDir` into the `current_dir` call would result in the `TempDir` being converted into
an internal representation, with the original value being dropped and the directory thus
being deleted, before the command can be executed.

The `touch` command would fail with an `No such file or directory` error.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Create a temporary file and write some data into it:

```
use tempfile::tempfile;
use std::io::Write;
// Create a file inside of `env::temp_dir()`.
let mut file = tempfile()?;
writeln!(file, "Brian was here. Briefly.")?;
```
Create a named temporary file and open an independent file handle:

```
use tempfile::NamedTempFile;
use std::io::{Write, Read};
let text = "Brian was here. Briefly.";
// Create a file inside of `env::temp_dir()`.
let mut file1 = NamedTempFile::new()?;
// Re-open it.
let mut file2 = file1.reopen()?;
// Write some test data to the first handle.
file1.write_all(text.as_bytes())?;
// Read the test data using the second handle.
let mut buf = String::new();
file2.read_to_string(&mut buf)?;
assert_eq!(buf, text);
```
Create a temporary directory and add a file to it:

```
use tempfile::tempdir;
use std::fs::File;
use std::io::Write;
// Create a directory inside of `env::temp_dir()`.
let dir = tempdir()?;
let file_path = dir.path().join("my-temporary-note.txt");
let mut file = File::create(file_path)?;
writeln!(file, "Brian was here. Briefly.")?;
// By closing the `TempDir` explicitly, we can check that it has
// been deleted successfully. If we don't close it explicitly,
// the directory will still be deleted when `dir` goes out
// of scope, but we won't know whether deleting the directory
// succeeded.
drop(file);
dir.close()?;
```

# cli_engine - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/cli-engine/0.3.5/target-redirect/cli_engine/

## Expand description

Build consistent, domain-oriented CLIs with a small amount of Rust.

`cli_engine` provides the shared pieces that most CLI tools need:
command registration, authentication provider routing, authorization hooks,
audit and activity hooks, structured output, output schemas, guides, search,
command tree rendering, busybox-style multi-call (`argv[0]`) dispatch, and
authenticated HTTP transport helpers.

The intended shape is:

- Each team owns one or more `Module`
- A module registers noun-based `GroupSpec`
- Groups contain verb-like `CommandSpec`
- Command handlers stay focused on domain behavior while `Middleware`

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

```
use clap::Arg;
use cli_engine::{
    BuildInfo, Cli, CliConfig, CommandSpec, GroupSpec, Module,
    RuntimeCommandSpec, RuntimeGroupSpec,
};
use serde_json::json;
#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> std::process::ExitCode {
    let list = RuntimeCommandSpec::new(
        CommandSpec::new("list", "List projects")
            .with_system("projects-api")
            .with_default_fields("id,name,status")
            .with_arg(Arg::new("team").long("team").required(true))
            .no_auth(true),
        async |_credential, args| {
            let team = args
                .get("team")
                .and_then(|value| value.as_str())
                .unwrap_or_default();
            Ok(cli_engine::CommandResult::new(json!([
                { "id": "p1", "name": "Portal", "status": "active", "team": team }
            ])))
        },
    );
    let module = Module::new("Platform Systems", move |_context| {
        RuntimeGroupSpec::new(GroupSpec::new("project", "Manage projects"))
            .with_command(list.clone())
    });
    let cli = Cli::new(
        CliConfig::new("example", "Example cli-engine application", "example")
            .with_build(BuildInfo::new(env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION")))
            .with_module(module),
    );
    cli.execute().await
}
```
Command paths are colon-separated (`project:list`) for policy, audit,
schema, and authorization compatibility with existing CLI ecosystems.

# cli_engine - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cli-engine/0.3.5/cli_engine/index.html

## Expand description

Build consistent, domain-oriented CLIs with a small amount of Rust.

`cli_engine` provides the shared pieces that most CLI tools need:
command registration, authentication provider routing, authorization hooks,
audit and activity hooks, structured output, output schemas, guides, search,
command tree rendering, busybox-style multi-call (`argv[0]`) dispatch, and
authenticated HTTP transport helpers.

The intended shape is:

- Each team owns one or more `Module`
- A module registers noun-based `GroupSpec`
- Groups contain verb-like `CommandSpec`
- Command handlers stay focused on domain behavior while `Middleware`

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

```
use clap::Arg;
use cli_engine::{
    BuildInfo, Cli, CliConfig, CommandSpec, GroupSpec, Module,
    RuntimeCommandSpec, RuntimeGroupSpec,
};
use serde_json::json;
#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> std::process::ExitCode {
    let list = RuntimeCommandSpec::new(
        CommandSpec::new("list", "List projects")
            .with_system("projects-api")
            .with_default_fields("id,name,status")
            .with_arg(Arg::new("team").long("team").required(true))
            .no_auth(true),
        async |_credential, args| {
            let team = args
                .get("team")
                .and_then(|value| value.as_str())
                .unwrap_or_default();
            Ok(cli_engine::CommandResult::new(json!([
                { "id": "p1", "name": "Portal", "status": "active", "team": team }
            ])))
        },
    );
    let module = Module::new("Platform Systems", move |_context| {
        RuntimeGroupSpec::new(GroupSpec::new("project", "Manage projects"))
            .with_command(list.clone())
    });
    let cli = Cli::new(
        CliConfig::new("example", "Example cli-engine application", "example")
            .with_build(BuildInfo::new(env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION")))
            .with_module(module),
    );
    cli.execute().await
}
```
Command paths are colon-separated (`project:list`) for policy, audit,
schema, and authorization compatibility with existing CLI ecosystems.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [auth](https://docs.rs/auth/index.html)
- Auth provider traits, dispatch, and built-in provider commands. Auth provider abstraction and built-in auth helpers.
- [cli](https://docs.rs/cli/index.html)
- CLI application assembly and execution.
- [command](https://docs.rs/command/index.html)
- Command and command-group specifications.
- [config](https://docs.rs/config/index.html)
- Engine config file and credential-storage selection. Engine configuration file and credential-storage selection.
- [config_](https://docs.rs/config_commands/index.html)- commands
- Built-in `config`command group. Built-in`config`command group for reading and writing the per-application[config file](https://docs.rs/config/struct.ConfigFile.html).
- [environments](https://docs.rs/environments/index.html)
- First-class environment definitions and layered resolution. First-class environment definitions and layered resolution.
- [error](https://docs.rs/error/index.html)
- Shared error type and error traits.
- [flags](https://docs.rs/flags/index.html)
- Global framework flags and flag-extraction helpers.
- [fs](https://docs.rs/fs/index.html)
- Filesystem and path utilities (base dir, path-component safety, atomic write). Filesystem and path utilities shared across the engine.
- [guide](https://docs.rs/guide/index.html)
- Embedded or file-backed guide parsing.
- [middleware](https://docs.rs/middleware/index.html)
- Cross-cutting command execution middleware.
- [module](https://docs.rs/module/index.html)
- Domain module registration helpers.
- [output](https://docs.rs/output/index.html)
- Structured output envelopes, renderers, schemas, and field projection. Structured output envelopes and renderers.
- [search](https://docs.rs/search/index.html)
- Search indexing for commands, guides, and extra documents.
- [tier](https://docs.rs/tier/index.html)
- Command risk tiers used by authentication, authorization, and dry-run.
- [transport](https://docs.rs/transport/index.html)
- HTTP transport client and auth injectors. HTTP transport helpers for command implementations.
- [tree](https://docs.rs/tree/index.html)
- Command tree data model and human rendering.

# lib.rs - source

Source: https://docs.rs/cli-engine/0.3.5/src/cli_engine/lib.rs.html

# cli_engine/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)//! Build consistent, domain-oriented CLIs with a small amount of Rust.
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//!
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//! `cli_engine` provides the shared pieces that most CLI tools need:
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//! command registration, authentication provider routing, authorization hooks,
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//! audit and activity hooks, structured output, output schemas, guides, search,
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//! command tree rendering, busybox-style multi-call (`argv[0]`) dispatch, and
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//! authenticated HTTP transport helpers.
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//!
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//! The intended shape is:
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//!
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//! 1. Each team owns one or more [`Module`] values.
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//! 2. A module registers noun-based [`GroupSpec`] groups.
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//! 3. Groups contain verb-like [`CommandSpec`] leaf commands.
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//! 4. Command handlers stay focused on domain behavior while [`Middleware`]
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//!    handles authentication, dry-run, audit, activity, output, and errors.
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//!
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//! # Quick Start
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//!
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//! ```no_run
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//! use clap::Arg;
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//! use cli_engine::{
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//!     BuildInfo, Cli, CliConfig, CommandSpec, GroupSpec, Module,
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//!     RuntimeCommandSpec, RuntimeGroupSpec,
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//! };
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//! use serde_json::json;
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//!
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//! #[tokio::main]
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//! async fn main() -> std::process::ExitCode {
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//!     let list = RuntimeCommandSpec::new(
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//!         CommandSpec::new("list", "List projects")
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//!             .with_system("projects-api")
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//!             .with_default_fields("id,name,status")
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//!             .with_arg(Arg::new("team").long("team").required(true))
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//!             .no_auth(true),
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//!         async |_credential, args| {
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//!             let team = args
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//!                 .get("team")
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//!                 .and_then(|value| value.as_str())
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//!                 .unwrap_or_default();
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//!             Ok(cli_engine::CommandResult::new(json!([
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//!                 { "id": "p1", "name": "Portal", "status": "active", "team": team }
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//!             ])))
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//!         },
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//!     );
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//!
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//!     let module = Module::new("Platform Systems", move |_context| {
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//!         RuntimeGroupSpec::new(GroupSpec::new("project", "Manage projects"))
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//!             .with_command(list.clone())
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//!     });
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//!
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//!     let cli = Cli::new(
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//!         CliConfig::new("example", "Example cli-engine application", "example")
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//!             .with_build(BuildInfo::new(env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION")))
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//!             .with_module(module),
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//!     );
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//!
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//!     cli.execute().await
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//! }
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//! ```
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//!
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//! Command paths are colon-separated (`project:list`) for policy, audit,
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//! schema, and authorization compatibility with existing CLI ecosystems.
[63](https://docs.rs#63)

[66](https://docs.rs#66)/// CLI application assembly and execution.

pub struct Module {
    pub category:
```
[String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html),
    pub guides: [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[GuideEntry](https://docs.rs/guide/struct.GuideEntry.html)>,
    pub views: [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[HumanViewDef](https://docs.rs/output/struct.HumanViewDef.html)>,
    pub register: [ModuleRegister](https://docs.rs/type.ModuleRegister.html),
}## Expand description

Domain-bounded unit of CLI functionality.

A module usually maps to a product, platform, resource family, or team ownership boundary. It contributes one top-level group plus optional guides and human output views.

## Fields[§](https://docs.rs#fields)

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.category)

`category: `[String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)Root help category.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.guides)

`guides: `[Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[GuideEntry](https://docs.rs/guide/struct.GuideEntry.html)>Guide entries merged into the CLI-wide guide command.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.views)

`views: `[Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[HumanViewDef](https://docs.rs/output/struct.HumanViewDef.html)>Human output views registered before command execution.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.register)

`register: `[ModuleRegister](https://docs.rs/type.ModuleRegister.html)Registration function that returns the module’s runtime group.

Declarative command group metadata.

Groups are noun-based containers. They do not run business logic directly; when invoked bare, the CLI renders group help.

## Fields[§](https://docs.rs#fields)

# CommandSpec in cli_engine::command - Rust

}## Expand description

Declarative leaf command metadata and parser arguments.

`CommandSpec` intentionally keeps command metadata next to the command’s
handler. This is the primary copy/paste surface for teams adding commands.

### impl [CommandSpec](https://docs.rs/struct.CommandSpec.html)

Creates a command spec with the required name and one-line help.

Creates a command spec from a `#[derive(clap::Args)]` struct.

Extracts the argument definitions from the derive type and populates the
spec’s args list. The command name and help text are still required since
`Args` types do not carry those.

Hides or shows this command in discovery output.

Assigns an inline human-output table view to this command.

The columns are registered under the command’s own path, so human output
renders this table directly. Field selection still applies: `--fields`
(defaulting to [ default_fields](https://docs.rs/struct.CommandSpec.html#structfield.default_fields)) narrows
which of these columns show. Use

[instead to point at a shared view registered with](https://docs.rs/struct.CommandSpec.html#method.with_view_id)

`with_view_id``with_view` on the module or CLI.[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cli_engine/command.rs.html#366-369)#### pub fn [with_view_id](https://docs.rs#method.with_view_id)(self, id: impl [Into](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.Into.html)<[String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)>) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cli_engine/command.rs.html#366-369)

#### pub fn [with_view_id](https://docs.rs#method.with_view_id)(self, id: impl [Into](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.Into.html)<[String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)>) -> Self

Points this command at a shared human view by id.

The id must match a [ HumanViewDef](https://docs.rs/output/struct.HumanViewDef.html) registered with

`with_view` on the module or CLI, letting several commands share one
table. Takes precedence over inline [columns.](https://docs.rs/struct.CommandSpec.html#method.with_view)

Selects the auth provider for this command.

Marks the command as no-auth.

`no_auth(true)` sets [ AuthRequirement::None](https://docs.rs/middleware/enum.AuthRequirement.html#variant.None): the command never resolves
a credential and default-env injection is suppressed.

`no_auth(false)`
restores the default [.](https://docs.rs/middleware/enum.AuthRequirement.html#variant.Required)

`AuthRequirement::Required`[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cli_engine/command.rs.html#407-410)#### pub fn [auth_optional](https://docs.rs#method.auth_optional)(self) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cli_engine/command.rs.html#407-410)

#### pub fn [auth_optional](https://docs.rs#method.auth_optional)(self) -> Self

Marks authentication as optional ([ AuthRequirement::Optional](https://docs.rs/middleware/enum.AuthRequirement.html#variant.Optional)).

The engine does not resolve a credential before the handler runs; the
handler triggers the auth flow only by calling
[ CredentialResolver::resolve](https://docs.rs/middleware/struct.CredentialResolver.html#method.resolve)/

[. Use for commands that should still run when the user is logged out.](https://docs.rs/middleware/struct.CredentialResolver.html#method.try_resolve)

`try_resolve`Adds provider-specific auth metadata.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cli_engine/command.rs.html#434-448)

Declares the OAuth scopes this command requires.

Sugar over [ with_auth_metadata](https://docs.rs/struct.CommandSpec.html#method.with_auth_metadata) with the

`"scopes"` key (whitespace-joined). The scopes surface on
[and reach the auth provider via](https://docs.rs/middleware/struct.CommandMeta.html)

`CommandMeta::scopes`[; a provider that supports scope step-up re-authenticates when the cached token lacks them.](https://docs.rs/auth/struct.CredentialRequest.html)

}## Expand description

Cross-cutting command execution state and dependencies.

Middleware is intentionally a plain, cloneable struct so tests and command
handlers can inspect what will be used for a run. Application setup usually
mutates it through `CliConfig` hooks or `ModuleContext`.

`config: `[Arc](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/sync/struct.Arc.html)<[ConfigFile](https://docs.rs/config/struct.ConfigFile.html)>Loaded per-application config file, shared across the run.

Populated once at startup from `<config-base>/<app_id>/config.toml`.
Command handlers read it via
[ CommandContext::config](https://docs.rs/command/struct.CommandContext.html#method.config) and
module registration via

[.](https://docs.rs/module/struct.ModuleContext.html#method.config)

Set by [ CliConfig::with_environments](https://docs.rs/cli/struct.CliConfig.html#method.with_environments)
and cloned into each per-run middleware snapshot. Handlers resolve the

# CredentialKey in cli_engine::auth::storage - Rust

```
pub struct CredentialKey<'key> {
    pub app_id: &'key
```
[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html),
    pub provider: &'key [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html),
    pub env: &'key [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html),
}## Expand description

Identifies a single stored credential.

Backends derive their storage location from this key: the keychain service
name and the file path are both functions of `(app_id, provider, env)`.

}## Expand description

A pluggable place to persist a provider’s serialized credential.

Values are opaque strings (typically JSON); the backend never interprets them, so it stays independent of any provider’s token shape. Callers own (de)serialization and any validity/expiry checks.

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cli_engine/auth/storage.rs.html#68)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cli_engine/auth/storage.rs.html#68)

Loads the stored blob for `key`, or `None` when absent or unreadable.

Backends own the policy for distinguishing “no entry” from “store
unavailable” (see `AutoStorage`); both collapse to `None` here.

# FileStorage in cli_engine::auth::storage - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cli-engine/0.3.5/cli_engine/auth/storage/struct.FileStorage.html

`pub struct FileStorage;`## Expand description

Unencrypted file-based credential storage.

Stores each credential as JSON at
`<config-base>/<app>/credentials/<provider>-<env>.json`, where `<app>` is the
key’s `app_id` (or `provider` when `app_id` is empty) and `<config-base>` is
resolved by [ config_base_dir](https://docs.rs/fs/fn.config_base_dir.html). On Unix the file is created

`0600` and the
parent directory is best-effort restricted to `0700`.Credentials are written in clear text, so prefer the system keychain where one is available.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

## Trait Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#trait-implementations)

}## Expand description

Named auth provider used by middleware and transport injectors.

Implementations own their credential cache strategy. The framework only
routes calls and passes command context (`env`, colon command path, and tier).

#### fn [get_credential_for](https://docs.rs#method.get_credential_for)<'life0, 'life1, 'life2, 'async_trait>(
    &'life0 self,
    req: &'life1 [CredentialRequest](https://docs.rs/struct.CredentialRequest.html)<'life2>,
) -> [Pin](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/pin/struct.Pin.html)<[Box](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/boxed/struct.Box.html)<dyn [Future](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/future/future/trait.Future.html)<Output = [Result](https://docs.rs/error/type.Result.html)<[Credential](https://docs.rs/struct.Credential.html)>> + [Send](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Send.html) + 'async_trait>>where
    Self: 'async_trait,
    'life0: 'async_trait,
    'life1: 'async_trait,
    'life2: 'async_trait,

Returns a credential for a command, given its full [ CredentialRequest](https://docs.rs/struct.CredentialRequest.html).

The default implementation ignores the metadata and delegates to
[ get_credential](https://docs.rs/trait.AuthProvider.html#tymethod.get_credential). Providers that act on
command metadata — such as an OAuth provider performing scope step-up
from

[— override this. The framework calls this method (not](https://docs.rs/middleware/struct.CommandMeta.html#structfield.scopes)

`CommandMeta::scopes``get_credential`) when resolving credentials, so an override
receives the command’s metadata.## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait **is** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

Reports whether the credential is expired.

Invalid `expires_at` values are treated as expired. Credentials without
either `expires_at` or `cached_at` are treated as not expired.

# CredentialRequest in cli_engine::auth - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cli-engine/0.3.5/cli_engine/auth/struct.CredentialRequest.html

```
#[non_exhaustive]pub struct CredentialRequest<'req> {
    pub env: &'req
```
[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html),
    pub command: &'req [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html),
    pub tier: &'req [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html),
    pub meta: &'req [CommandMeta](https://docs.rs/middleware/struct.CommandMeta.html),
}## Expand description

Everything an [ AuthProvider](https://docs.rs/trait.AuthProvider.html) may inspect about the command requesting a
credential.

This bundles the routing fields passed to [ AuthProvider::get_credential](https://docs.rs/trait.AuthProvider.html#tymethod.get_credential)
(

`env`, colon command path, and tier) together with the command’s
[, so a provider can read richer metadata — for example an OAuth provider reading](https://docs.rs/middleware/struct.CommandMeta.html)

`CommandMeta`[to decide whether the cached token is sufficient. Providers that do not need metadata can ignore it.](https://docs.rs/middleware/struct.CommandMeta.html#structfield.scopes)

`CommandMeta::scopes`Marked `#[non_exhaustive]` because the framework constructs it (providers only
read it) and more request fields may be added over time; build one with
[ CredentialRequest::new](https://docs.rs/struct.CredentialRequest.html#method.new) rather than a struct literal so adding a field is
not a breaking change for downstream crates.

## Fields (Non-exhaustive)[§](https://docs.rs#fields)

## This struct is marked as non-exhaustive

# Dispatcher in cli_engine::auth - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cli-engine/0.3.5/cli_engine/auth/struct.Dispatcher.html

`pub struct Dispatcher { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Routes auth operations to registered providers by name.

Clones share the same provider registry, so provider facades and transport injectors see later registration or replacement.

# ApplyFlags in cli_engine::cli - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cli-engine/0.3.5/cli_engine/cli/type.ApplyFlags.html

# Argv0LinkMethod in cli_engine::cli - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cli-engine/0.3.5/cli_engine/cli/enum.Argv0LinkMethod.html

```
#[non_exhaustive]pub enum Argv0LinkMethod {
    SoftLink,
    HardLink,
    Script,
}
```
## Expand description

On-disk mechanism used by [ Cli::create_link](https://docs.rs/struct.Cli.html#method.create_link) to materialize an alternative

`argv[0]` name so the binary can be invoked under it.Installers pick the mechanism that suits the platform and environment;
self-healing code can re-run [ Cli::create_link](https://docs.rs/struct.Cli.html#method.create_link) to restore a deleted link.

Non-exhaustive: more link mechanisms may be added in future releases.

## Variants (Non-exhaustive)[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

## This enum is marked as non-exhaustive

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.SoftLink)

### SoftLink

A symbolic link to the target executable (`<name>` on Unix, `<name>.exe`
on Windows). On Windows this may require Developer Mode or elevation.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.HardLink)

### HardLink

A hard link to the target executable (`<name>` on Unix, `<name>.exe` on
Windows). The link must live on the same volume as the target.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Script)

### Script

A small shim script that forwards to the target via the `argv0` command:
a `<name>.cmd` batch file on Windows, or an executable `<name>` shell
script on Unix. Useful when links are unavailable or inconvenient.

# Argv0Route in cli_engine::cli - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cli-engine/0.3.5/cli_engine/cli/enum.Argv0Route.html

```
#[non_exhaustive]pub enum Argv0Route {
    Alias(
```
[Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)>),
    Personality([Arc](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/sync/struct.Arc.html)<dyn [Fn](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/function/trait.Fn.html)() -> [CliConfig](https://docs.rs/struct.CliConfig.html) + [Send](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Send.html) + [Sync](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sync.html)>),
}## Expand description

How the engine behaves when invoked under a registered alternative `argv[0]`
name (busybox/git-style multi-call dispatch).

A route is selected when the binary’s `argv[0]` basename — or the name given
to the hidden `argv0` command — matches a key registered via
[ CliConfig::with_argv0_alias](https://docs.rs/struct.CliConfig.html#method.with_argv0_alias) or

[. An](https://docs.rs/struct.CliConfig.html#method.with_argv0_personality)

`CliConfig::with_argv0_personality``argv[0]` that matches no route falls through to the default CLI, so existing
applications that register no routes are unaffected.Non-exhaustive: more route kinds may be added in future releases. Register
routes through the [ CliConfig](https://docs.rs/struct.CliConfig.html) builders rather than matching on variants.

## Variants (Non-exhaustive)[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

## This enum is marked as non-exhaustive

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Alias)

Rewrite the invocation into these canonical subcommand tokens and run it through the normal command tree, with the real argument tail appended.

For example, an `Alias(vec!["project".into(), "list".into()])` registered
under `pl` makes `pl --team x` behave exactly like `project list --team x`.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Personality)

Run an entirely separate CLI application built from the returned
[ CliConfig](https://docs.rs/struct.CliConfig.html) (its own root name, commands, flags, and auth). The
configuration is built lazily, only when the route is actually dispatched,
so registering a personality costs nothing for invocations that never hit it.

## Trait Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#trait-implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cli_engine/cli.rs.html#1122-1138)#### pub fn [add_guides](https://docs.rs#method.add_guides)(
    &mut self,
    entries: impl [IntoIterator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/collect/trait.IntoIterator.html)<Item = [GuideEntry](https://docs.rs/guide/struct.GuideEntry.html)>,
) -> &mut Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cli_engine/cli.rs.html#1122-1138)

#### pub fn [add_guides](https://docs.rs#method.add_guides)(
    &mut self,
    entries: impl [IntoIterator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/collect/trait.IntoIterator.html)<Item = [GuideEntry](https://docs.rs/guide/struct.GuideEntry.html)>,
) -> &mut Self

Adds guide entries after construction.

Creates an on-disk link in `dir` that lets the binary be invoked under the
registered alternative `argv[0]` name `name`, using `method`.

`target` is the executable the link points at; pass `None` to use the
current executable ([ std::env::current_exe](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/env/fn.current_exe.html)), which is the common choice
for install and self-healing code. The file name follows the platform and
method: a symlink or hard link is

`<name>` on Unix and `<name>.exe` on
Windows; a [shim is](https://docs.rs/enum.Argv0LinkMethod.html#variant.Script)

`Argv0LinkMethod::Script``<name>.cmd` on Windows and
an executable `<name>` shell script on Unix.The call ensures the desired state idempotently: if the destination already
matches what would be created (a symlink to `target`, a hard link with the
same contents, or a shim with identical contents) it is left untouched and
its path returned; if it exists but differs (wrong kind, stale target, or
edited shim) it is replaced. This makes the call safe to re-run as install
or self-healing code, restoring both deleted and corrupted links. The
directory is created if necessary.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

Returns an error if `name` is not a registered route, if the current
executable cannot be resolved (when `target` is `None`), or if the
directory or link cannot be created or replaced (e.g. insufficient
privilege for a Windows symlink, or a hard link across volumes).

}## Expand description

Declarative configuration for a CLI application.

Use [ CliConfig::new](https://docs.rs/struct.CliConfig.html#method.new) for the common path and chain

`with_*` methods for
modules, auth providers, guides, views, and lifecycle hooks. Direct struct
literals remain available for advanced setup and tests.## Fields[§](https://docs.rs#fields)

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.name)

`name: `[String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)Root command name shown in usage output.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.short)

`short: `[String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)One-line root command description.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.long)

`long: `[Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)>Optional longer root command description. Defaults to `short`.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.build)

`build: `[BuildInfo](https://docs.rs/struct.BuildInfo.html)Version/build metadata for `--version`.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.app_id)

`app_id: `[String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)Application id stored in middleware and output metadata.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.default_auth_provider)

`default_auth_provider: `[Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)>Fallback auth provider when a command does not select one explicitly.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.modules)

`modules: `[Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[Module](https://docs.rs/module/struct.Module.html)>Domain modules mounted under the root command.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.commands)

of the built-in sensitive set (`authorization`, `proxy-authorization`,
`cookie`, `set-cookie`, `x-api-key`). Set CLI-specific secret-bearing
headers here — e.g. a custom API-key header an auth injector adds.

command under this heading; apps should use the same name for their own
admin modules (e.g. godaddy’s `env`). When unset, defaults to `"Admin"`;
set it to match a consumer’s own taxonomy (e.g. gdx’s “Administration”).

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.config_commands)

`config_commands: `[bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)Whether to mount the built-in `config` command group (`config get`/`set`/`path`/`list`). Off by default to avoid colliding with a
consumer’s own `config` noun. Enable via
[ CliConfig::with_config_commands](https://docs.rs/struct.CliConfig.html#method.with_config_commands).

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.argv0_routes)

`argv0_routes: `[BTreeMap](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/collections/btree/map/struct.BTreeMap.html)<[String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html), [Argv0Route](https://docs.rs/enum.Argv0Route.html)>Alternative `argv[0]` names this binary may be invoked as, mapped to the
behavior the engine should take (busybox/git-style multi-call dispatch).

Keyed by the bare alternative name (no path, no extension). Empty by
default, in which case argv0 dispatch is inert and behavior is identical
to a binary that never opted in. Populate via [ CliConfig::with_argv0_alias](https://docs.rs/struct.CliConfig.html#method.with_argv0_alias)
and

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.CliConfig.html#method.with_argv0_personality)

`CliConfig::with_argv0_personality`[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.environments)

Overrides the outbound User-Agent string for all HTTP traffic.

When unset, the engine derives `name/version` from this config (see
[ CliConfig::user_agent_string](https://docs.rs/struct.CliConfig.html#method.user_agent_string)). Set this when the upstream APIs expect
a specific product token. The resolved value is applied process-wide on
execution via

[, so it reaches both command](https://docs.rs/transport/client/fn.set_default_user_agent.html)

`crate::transport::set_default_user_agent`[s and the engine’s own OAuth token requests.](https://docs.rs/transport/client/struct.HttpClient.html)

`HttpClient`[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cli_engine/cli.rs.html#378-388)#### pub fn [with_redacted_debug_headers](https://docs.rs#method.with_redacted_debug_headers)(
    self,
    names: impl [IntoIterator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/collect/trait.IntoIterator.html)<Item = impl [Into](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.Into.html)<[String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)>>,
) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cli_engine/cli.rs.html#378-388)

#### pub fn [with_redacted_debug_headers](https://docs.rs#method.with_redacted_debug_headers)(
    self,
    names: impl [IntoIterator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/collect/trait.IntoIterator.html)<Item = impl [Into](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.Into.html)<[String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)>>,
) -> Self

Adds HTTP header names to redact in `--debug transport` output, on top of
the built-in sensitive set.

Use this for CLI-specific secret-bearing headers that are not standard
auth headers — for example a custom API-key header that an
[ AuthInjector](https://docs.rs/transport/injector/trait.AuthInjector.html) sets. Matching is
case-insensitive and additive: the built-in set is always redacted.
Calls accumulate. Names are trimmed and empty entries are dropped, so a
mistyped value with stray whitespace cannot silently disable redaction.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cli_engine/cli.rs.html#397-406)#### pub fn [user_agent_string](https://docs.rs#method.user_agent_string)(&self) -> [String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cli_engine/cli.rs.html#397-406)

#### pub fn [user_agent_string](https://docs.rs#method.user_agent_string)(&self) -> [String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)

Returns the outbound User-Agent string the CLI presents on HTTP requests.

Resolution order:

- an explicit `with_user_agent`
- otherwise `name/version`(for example`gdx/1.2.3`);
- otherwise just `name`when no build version is set.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cli_engine/cli.rs.html#417-420)#### pub fn [with_module](https://docs.rs#method.with_module)(self, module: [Module](https://docs.rs/module/struct.Module.html)) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cli_engine/cli.rs.html#417-420)

#### pub fn [with_module](https://docs.rs#method.with_module)(self, module: [Module](https://docs.rs/module/struct.Module.html)) -> Self

Adds one domain module.

[§](https://docs.rs#reserved-group-names)Reserved group names

The top-level group names `help`, `guide`, `tree`, and `completion` are
reserved by the engine.  A module whose root group uses one of these
names will be rejected at registration time (logged as a warning) so
the engine’s own built-in always takes precedence in the command tree.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cli_engine/cli.rs.html#547-550)#### pub fn [with_admin_category](https://docs.rs#method.with_admin_category)(self, category: impl [Into](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.Into.html)<[String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)>) -> Self

#### pub fn [with_admin_category](https://docs.rs#method.with_admin_category)(self, category: impl [Into](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.Into.html)<[String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)>) -> Self

Sets the name of the admin help category. The engine files the built-in
`auth` command there; apps should use the same name for their own admin
modules (e.g. godaddy’s `env`). Optional: defaults to `"Admin"`.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cli_engine/cli.rs.html#558-561)#### pub fn [with_config_commands](https://docs.rs#method.with_config_commands)(self) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cli_engine/cli.rs.html#558-561)

#### pub fn [with_config_commands](https://docs.rs#method.with_config_commands)(self) -> Self

Mounts the built-in `config` command group (`config get`/`set`/`path`/
`list`) for reading and writing the per-application config file.

Off by default so it never collides with a consumer’s own `config` noun;
the group is filed under the admin help category when enabled.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cli_engine/cli.rs.html#586-604)#### pub fn [with_argv0_alias](https://docs.rs#method.with_argv0_alias)(
    self,
    name: impl [Into](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.Into.html)<[String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)>,
    command_path: impl [IntoIterator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/collect/trait.IntoIterator.html)<Item = impl [Into](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.Into.html)<[String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)>>,
) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cli_engine/cli.rs.html#586-604)

#### pub fn [with_argv0_alias](https://docs.rs#method.with_argv0_alias)(
    self,
    name: impl [Into](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.Into.html)<[String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)>,
    command_path: impl [IntoIterator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/collect/trait.IntoIterator.html)<Item = impl [Into](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.Into.html)<[String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)>>,
) -> Self

Registers an alternative `argv[0]` name that acts as a shortcut to a
command path on this same CLI.

When the binary is invoked under `name` (via symlink, hardlink, copy, or
the hidden `argv0` command), the engine behaves as if the user had typed
`command_path` followed by the real argument tail, routed through the
normal command tree. For example:

```
use cli_engine::CliConfig;
// Invoking the binary as `pl --team platform` runs `project list --team platform`.
let config = CliConfig::new("my-cli", "Team CLI", "my-cli")
    .with_argv0_alias("pl", ["project", "list"]);
```
`name` must be a simple token: non-empty and composed only of ASCII
letters, digits, `-`, or `_` (no dots, spaces, path separators, or shell
metacharacters), and it must differ from the CLI’s own name. These are
debug-asserted. The restriction keeps the name usable as a link/shim
filename and an `argv[0]` basename (which is matched with its extension
stripped, so a dot would break matching).

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cli_engine/cli.rs.html#628-646)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cli_engine/cli.rs.html#628-646)

Registers an alternative `argv[0]` name that runs an entirely separate CLI
application.

When the binary is invoked under `name`, the engine builds a fresh
[ CliConfig](https://docs.rs/struct.CliConfig.html) from

`build` and runs that application instead — its own root
name, commands, flags, and auth. The closure runs lazily, only when the
route is dispatched, so unused personalities cost nothing. The personality
presents the name from its own [in help and usage output.](https://docs.rs/struct.CliConfig.html)

`CliConfig````
use cli_engine::CliConfig;
let config = CliConfig::new("my-cli", "Team CLI", "my-cli")
    .with_argv0_personality("legacy-tool", || {
        CliConfig::new("legacy-tool", "Legacy compatibility shim", "legacy-tool")
    });
```
`name` follows the same contract as [ CliConfig::with_argv0_alias](https://docs.rs/struct.CliConfig.html#method.with_argv0_alias): a
simple

`[A-Za-z0-9_-]` token, differing from the CLI’s own name
(debug-asserted).## Trait Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#trait-implementations)

# CommandContext in cli_engine::command - Rust

```
#[non_exhaustive]pub struct CommandContext {
    pub credential:
```
[CredentialResolver](https://docs.rs/middleware/struct.CredentialResolver.html),
    pub args: [ValueMap](https://docs.rs/middleware/type.ValueMap.html),
    pub user_args: [ValueMap](https://docs.rs/middleware/type.ValueMap.html),
    pub command_path: [String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html),
    pub middleware: [Middleware](https://docs.rs/middleware/struct.Middleware.html),
    pub raw_matches: [Arc](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/sync/struct.Arc.html)<[ArgMatches](https://docs.rs/clap_builder/4.6.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/clap_builder/parser/matches/arg_matches/struct.ArgMatches.html)>,
}## Expand description

Runtime context passed to advanced command handlers.

Most commands can use [ RuntimeCommandSpec::new](https://docs.rs/struct.RuntimeCommandSpec.html#method.new) and receive just the
credential and effective args. Use this context when a command needs the
colon path, user-supplied args, or a snapshot of middleware state.

This struct is constructed by the framework during command dispatch. Consumer code receives it in handler closures and should not construct it directly.

## Fields (Non-exhaustive)[§](https://docs.rs#fields)

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.command_path)

#### pub fn [config](https://docs.rs#method.config)(&self) -> &[ConfigFile](https://docs.rs/config/struct.ConfigFile.html)

Returns the per-application config file as loaded at startup.

Read a consumer-owned section with
[ ConfigFile::section](https://docs.rs/config/struct.ConfigFile.html#method.section), for example

`ctx.config().section::<DeployConfig>("deploy")?`. Engine-reserved
settings are available via
[.](https://docs.rs/config/struct.ConfigFile.html#method.engine)

`ConfigFile::engine`**Snapshot semantics**: this is the config loaded once when
[ crate::cli::Cli::new](https://docs.rs/cli/struct.Cli.html#method.new) was called. Changes made by

`config set` during the same process
invocation (e.g. from a previous `Cli::run`) are not reflected here;
restart the CLI (a new `Cli::new`) to pick them up. For a one-shot CLI
process this is always the current on-disk state.[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cli_engine/command.rs.html#152-157)#### pub fn [environment](https://docs.rs#method.environment)(&self) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/error/type.Result.html)<[Environment](https://docs.rs/environments/struct.Environment.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cli_engine/command.rs.html#152-157)

#### pub fn [environment](https://docs.rs#method.environment)(&self) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/error/type.Result.html)<[Environment](https://docs.rs/environments/struct.Environment.html)>

Resolves the active [ Environment](https://docs.rs/environments/struct.Environment.html) for
this invocation.

The active environment name is `self.middleware.env`, seeded at startup
from the persisted active environment or configured default and
overridden per invocation by the global `--env` flag. Resolution merges
the compiled-in definition, the `environments.toml` file layer, and
`<ENV>_*` environment-variable overrides.

[§](https://docs.rs#blocking)Blocking

When the `environments.toml` file layer is enabled, this performs
synchronous filesystem I/O via
[ Environments::resolve](https://docs.rs/environments/struct.Environments.html#method.resolve).
Call it once per invocation and reuse the result rather than calling it
repeatedly inside an async handler on a latency-sensitive path.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

Returns an error if no environment system was registered via
[ CliConfig::with_environments](https://docs.rs/cli/struct.CliConfig.html#method.with_environments) or
if the active name does not resolve to a known environment.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cli_engine/command.rs.html#167-170)#### pub fn [typed_args](https://docs.rs#method.typed_args)<T: [FromArgMatches](https://docs.rs/clap_builder/4.6.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/clap_builder/derive/trait.FromArgMatches.html)>(&self) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/error/type.Result.html)<T>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cli_engine/command.rs.html#167-170)

#### pub fn [typed_args](https://docs.rs#method.typed_args)<T: [FromArgMatches](https://docs.rs/clap_builder/4.6.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/clap_builder/derive/trait.FromArgMatches.html)>(&self) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/error/type.Result.html)<T>

Deserializes the raw argument matches into a typed args struct.

Use this with `#[derive(clap::Args)]` structs to get type-safe access
to command arguments instead of working with the `ValueMap` directly.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors-1)Errors

Returns an error if the matches cannot be deserialized into `T`.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cli_engine/command.rs.html#218-220)#### pub async fn [credential_with_scopes](https://docs.rs#method.credential_with_scopes)(
    &self,
    extra: &[[String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)],
) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/error/type.Result.html)<[Credential](https://docs.rs/auth/struct.Credential.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cli_engine/command.rs.html#218-220)

#### pub async fn [credential_with_scopes](https://docs.rs#method.credential_with_scopes)(
    &self,
    extra: &[[String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)],
) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/error/type.Result.html)<[Credential](https://docs.rs/auth/struct.Credential.html)>

Resolves a credential that additionally covers `extra` scopes, on top of
the command’s declared scopes.

Use this when the required scopes are only known at runtime (for example a generic API caller that derives scopes from the target endpoint). A scope-aware auth provider re-authenticates when the cached token does not already cover the requested set.

Convenience wrapper over
[ self.credential.resolve_with_scopes()](https://docs.rs/middleware/struct.CredentialResolver.html#method.resolve_with_scopes).

If the handler also issues HTTP requests through the transport bearer
injector, call this **before** the first request: the injector resolves
and caches a scope-unaware token, so stepping up afterwards would not
affect requests it already authorized. See
[ CredentialResolver::resolve_with_scopes](https://docs.rs/middleware/struct.CredentialResolver.html#method.resolve_with_scopes) for the full ordering note.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors-4)Errors

Returns an error when the command is marked `no_auth`, or when the auth
provider fails to produce a credential.

Sets the application id used to locate the config file.

The consumer must set this to the same `app_id` passed to
[ CliConfig::new](https://docs.rs/cli/struct.CliConfig.html#method.new) before sharing the

[with both](https://docs.rs/struct.Environments.html)

`Environments`[and](https://docs.rs/cli/struct.CliConfig.html#method.with_environments)

`CliConfig::with_environments``PkceAuthProvider::with_environments` (with the `pkce-auth` feature),
or [returns](https://docs.rs/struct.Environments.html#method.config_file_path)

`config_file_path``None` and the
`environments.toml` file layer silently resolves empty.[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cli_engine/environments.rs.html#159-163)#### pub fn [with_config_file_path_override](https://docs.rs#method.with_config_file_path_override)(self, path: [PathBuf](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/path/struct.PathBuf.html)) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cli_engine/environments.rs.html#159-163)

#### pub fn [with_config_file_path_override](https://docs.rs#method.with_config_file_path_override)(self, path: [PathBuf](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/path/struct.PathBuf.html)) -> Self

Test/advanced seam: force the environments file path.

Enumerable environment names (compiled-in + file-defined), sorted.

Any error from reading or parsing the environments file (missing file,
permission/read error, or malformed TOML) is silently swallowed and only
the compiled-in names are returned. Use [ resolve](https://docs.rs/struct.Environments.html#method.resolve) when
you need those errors surfaced; a fallible listing variant can be added
later if needed.

[§](https://docs.rs#blocking)Blocking

When the config-file layer is enabled, this performs synchronous
filesystem I/O to read and parse `environments.toml` (like
[ resolve](https://docs.rs/struct.Environments.html#method.resolve)). Avoid calling it repeatedly on a
latency-sensitive async path.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cli_engine/environments.rs.html#214-241)#### pub fn [resolve](https://docs.rs#method.resolve)(&self, name: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/error/type.Result.html)<[Environment](https://docs.rs/struct.Environment.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cli_engine/environments.rs.html#214-241)

#### pub fn [resolve](https://docs.rs#method.resolve)(&self, name: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/error/type.Result.html)<[Environment](https://docs.rs/struct.Environment.html)>

Resolves `name` by merging compiled defaults, the config file,
and `<ENV>_*` env-var overrides (later wins) into an [ Environment](https://docs.rs/struct.Environment.html).

When only `client_id` was set on the matching layer(s), the returned
[ Environment](https://docs.rs/struct.Environment.html)’s

`oauth.auth_url` / `oauth.token_url` will be empty
strings. Consumers should treat empty endpoint strings as “fall back to
the provider’s default base endpoints”.[§](https://docs.rs#blocking-1)Blocking

When the config-file layer is enabled (via
[ with_config_file](https://docs.rs/struct.Environments.html#method.with_config_file)), this performs synchronous
filesystem I/O to read and parse

`environments.toml`. Resolve the
environment once at startup (or off the latency-sensitive path) rather
than calling it per request inside an async handler.[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

Returns an error when `name` is not known to any layer or when the
environments file exists but cannot be read or parsed.
